segments.text: This is an investigation into an object whose maker is not presently known.
The photograph before us shows a small robot: a face, a chassis, mechanisms arranged to be seen as well as to do work.
It has come to be called the Tati robot. That name is a handle for this inquiry. It is not an authorship claim.
We will not turn resemblance into proof. We will not let a good story fill a gap in the record.
For now, the photograph gives us only what a photograph can give.
There is a head. There are eyes. A jaw-like mechanism. A body with visible structure. Those are observations, not a diagnosis of how the machine worked, when it was made, or who made it.
The available provenance places the object in Paris. It does not, by itself, tell us the route by which it arrived there. Paris is a location in the file, not a nationality or a maker's signature.
An object can be collected, sold, moved, exhibited, or remembered far from the place where it was built. Until a source connects a person to this object, the maker field remains empty.
That emptiness is not a failure of the story. It is the condition of the story.

We can gather documents. We can compare documented machine cultures. We can say when a connection is an inference rather than a fact. And we can build transparent reconstructions to test a mechanical idea.
But a reconstruction is not testimony.
Nor is a plausible builder a proven builder.
The labels will stay on screen: documented, inference, reconstruction, unknown.
Our question is simple: what kind of world might have made this machine possible?
